title: Curtains
segment_text:
## Chapter 11 — Curtains

He came at twenty past ten with the curtains in two carrier bags and set them on the end of the table the way a man sets down a thing he has carried further than he meant to.

"I've been told you'll not do curtains."

"Who told you that?"

"The woman with the pies."

Alison looked at the bags. She had said it herself, on her second day, to Hilary, and had heard her own voice say it and had not stopped to look at the sound. *I don't do curtains.* There had been an edge on it. The edge had been fitted to her over twenty-six years on the fourth floor at Ellerby's, where curtains were soft furnishings and soft furnishings were not alterations, and everybody had known their place including the cloth.

She took a pair out. Lined cotton sateen, a leaf pattern in green and rust, chosen with care in a shop in about 1998 and chosen again every morning since. The drop was six inches out, perhaps seven.

"They came with the house?"

"They came with the window. New window, March. Fella took the old one out and the new one sits higher." He put his hands in his coat pockets. "So they've been down on the floor since. I've not moved owt in that room since March." He stopped. "I thought I'd start with the curtains."

Alison did not ask. She measured instead, along the table, then on her knees for the second pair, and wrote the drop on the back of a docket and read it out to him, and he said that sounded about right.

"Thirty-eight pounds," she said. "For the four. There's the lining to do as well as the face, and the weights to come out and go back in."

She made herself say the number with nothing on the end of it. It sat in the air of the hall, naked, and she did not go after it with a *but if that's too much*. He took out his wallet and counted three tens, a five and three pound coins onto the deal, the way you pay for a thing that costs what it costs.

"Thursday," she said.

"No rush." And then, at the north door: "There is a bit of a rush, actually. It's dark at teatime now."

There was no room on the table to check the hang, so she laid the first pair on the floor of the hall, six feet of lining on cold stone under the lanterns, and knelt at the top of it with her chalk. She was aware of being looked at. She carried on. Kelly, without a word and without stopping the milk she was steaming, put one hand on the end of the coffee cart and walked it eighteen inches towards pitch 7, and stood a bit narrower behind it for the rest of the day, and never mentioned it.

Alison worked from the floor with the chalk in her teeth. She was furious. Not with him. With the fourth floor, and with every hem she had ever priced at what she thought a woman would put up with.
cliffhanger: The lad with the football shirt will not say who signed it.

title: The Shoulder
segment_text:
## Chapter 12 — The Shoulder

He was nineteen and he had the shirt inside his coat rather than in a bag, which told her most of it before he opened his mouth.

"Sleeve's gone," he said. "There." He laid it out and turned it so the shoulder faced her, and put a finger near it and not on it.

A Town shirt, blue and white, the badge lifting at one corner. The seam at the sleeve-head had let go for four inches, the thread perished the way thread does when a shirt has been folded on the same fold for years. And across the shoulder, in marker faded from black to a warm brown, a signature: a great confident loop and a line ruled under it that ran nearly to the collar.

The ink crossed the seam. Of course it did.

"Who signed it?"

He looked at the badge. "Just someone."

"Right."

She turned it inside out and worked her thumb along the split. If she closed that seam the ordinary way, the needle would go through the tail of the signature nine times, and the marker would craze along the stitch line, and in a year the loop would have a dotted line through it like a coupon. She sat back and had a think, with her thumb going against her forefinger.

What she did in the end took fifty minutes. She dropped the sleeve out of the armhole entirely, which is not what you do, and worked from the wrong side with the shoulder laid flat over a rolled towel so the ink never came under tension. She used a fine ballpoint needle and shortened the stitch, and stopped a quarter-inch shy of the letters and picked the last of it up by hand from the reverse, catching one thread of the jersey at a time. Small stitches. Slow ones. The kind nobody sees, which is the kind she has spent her life on.

The hall got on with itself. Yusuf's wheel. Bernie's commentary. Margo playing something dreadful.

"Is it a player?" Alison said, halfway, not looking up. "Somebody good?"

"No." A long pause. She let it be long. "It's me grandad's. He signed it for me at Shay when I were seven. I asked him for his autograph and he did it, and me mum went spare because it were a new shirt." He rubbed the back of his neck. "It's daft."

"It's not daft."

"He's in a home at Elland now. I go Sundays."

"Right," said Alison, and put the needle in again, and said nothing else, because he had not come here to be talked to.

She finished it at ten to twelve and pressed the shoulder over the ham with the iron held an inch off and the steam doing the work. The loop sat exactly where it had sat. You could not find the seam unless you knew, and she knew, and she was not going to say.

"Five pounds," she said.

He carried it to the north light and held it up by the shoulders and photographed it. Then he turned the phone the other way round and did it again, and looked at the two, and sent one.

title: A Queue
segment_text:
## Chapter 13 — A Queue

At ten past nine there were three waiting and Alison assumed they were waiting for the cash machine by the north door, which has been broken since the spring.

They were not waiting for the cash machine.

Word had gone round. It goes round in a town that size the way water goes down a hill, by whatever route is open: the school gate, the queue at Bernie's, a woman telling another woman in the Co-op that there's a lass in the Lantern doing knees for four pound. By half past nine there were five. By ten there were eleven jobs in the building — on the table, on the floor, over the back of the chair, three of them in knotted bags with a name on a bit of paper inside, left by people who had not queued at all because they had assumed, correctly, that she would still be there.

She wrote them in a school exercise book in the hand she had used on Ellerby's dockets for twenty-six years. Name, garment, job, price, day. School trousers. A cuff. Another cuff. A zip in a fleece, which she should have refused and did not. Two prom dresses for October from the same family, the girls not speaking to one another. A pair of work trousers ripped clean across the seat, handed over folded with the rip turned in by a man who would not meet her eye, and she took them and said nothing at all and put three pounds in the book, and that was the correct thing to do.

The heat came at half past ten, the way it did now, arriving without knocking. Alison put the needle down before it reached her hands, because a needle does not care what your body is doing. She opened the north door two inches. Bernie, four stalls down, did not look up, and did not stop talking, and slid the little fan along the counter towards her.

By one o'clock she had stopped being frightened of the book. By two she was wrecked. Her back had gone at the top, between the shoulder blades, in the place that had had a chair fitted to it for a quarter of a century and now had a stool with no back on it. She ate half a pie standing at the machine with her left hand and could not afterwards have told anybody what was in it.

She was a business. That was the thing that sat oddly. Not that she was busy — she had always been busy; being busy had been done to her by other people since 1990. It was that the money was hers and the mistakes would be hers and the day was a thing she had made herself, out of a table nobody had wanted for two years, under the worst of the draught.

At five to four the queue was still four deep. She looked up between two hems to see how much of it was left, and at the end of it, patient, in her coat, with the ring of thirty-one keys in her hand and not a stitch of anything to be mended, stood Hilary Ashworth, waiting her turn.
cliffhanger: There is an envelope in Hilary's office that she has not opened for six days.

title: The Envelope
segment_text:
## Chapter 14 — The Envelope

The envelope had been on Hilary's desk since the Wednesday, propped against the tin where the fire-door keys live. She had not opened it. She had not put it in a drawer either, which Alison thought afterwards was the most honest thing about it.

Ivan Prewitt came at two. Forty-odd, in a coat bought for a different job, carrying a clipboard the way a man carries an umbrella he does not believe in. He said good afternoon to the hall in general and the hall in general looked at him.

They got twenty people into a back office with room for nine. Bernie stood in the doorway. Margo sat on the filing cabinet and did not apologise for it. Alison stood at the back by the kettle, and had a clear thought, which was that she had been trading for nineteen days and had no business being in this room, and stayed.

He read out numbers he had not written. That was the thing she could not stop noticing: the man was reading. Thirty-one pitches. Twenty-two let. A footfall figure from a count done on a wet Tuesday in February, which Bernie had views on. The roof: eleven lanterns, four of them gone, a leak over pitch 7 that had been on a list since 2019 and had rained on Ken's cards for seven winters. Fourteen months remaining on the lease. And an operator — he used that word, operator, twice, and heard himself use it the second time — interested in the ground floor. Which was to say the hall. Which was to say all of them.

"Interested in what way?" said Sonia.

"Flexible retail and leisure."

"What's that when it's at home?"

"I don't know," Ivan said. "I genuinely don't. It's not my wording."

And he put the sheet down on the desk, face up, so anybody could read it, which was not what a man defending a document does.

Nobody shouted. Alison had expected shouting and there was none, and the absence of it was worse. Margo asked what date. Yusuf asked, very quietly, whether a decision had been taken already and they were being told, and Ivan said no, and then said, more slowly, that he could not promise what a committee would do in fourteen months but that nothing had been decided, and that he would rather say that than say something comfortable.

Hilary said almost nothing. She read the lease clause he pointed at, aloud, in a voice that gave nothing away, the way she reads everything.

Alison stood by the kettle with her thumb going against her forefinger. Nineteen days. She had a table, and a book with eleven jobs in it, and a hall that had started saying her name without her surname, and a hot pie once a week she was not allowed to pay for, and the whole of it had a date on it now, the way the fourth floor had had a date on it, and nobody had told her that either until April.

When the room emptied, Hilary put her keys down on the desk between them. Thirty-one, on a steel ring. Three of them open nothing at all.
cliffhanger: A woman is coming in the morning with a dress she cannot fasten, and it has been in the boot of her car for a year.

title: Seam Allowance
segment_text:
## Chapter 15 — Seam Allowance

The dress came in a carrier bag that had been folded down and folded down again over a year, until the top of it had gone soft and grey as a dishcloth.

"It's been in the boot," the woman said. Fifty-five or so, good coat, and she said it lightly, in the voice of somebody delivering a line she has practised in a car. "I don't know what I think's going to happen to it. I've ruined it, is what it is."

Alison took it out. Green — a proper green, wool crepe with weight in it — bought in 2019 for a day that had mattered, which she knew because nobody drives a dress about for a year over a day that did not.

"What is it you can't do with it?"

"It won't fasten," the woman said, and laughed.

Alison turned the dress inside out on the table. She laid the side seam flat under her hand and ran her thumb — the flat one, the one that has been pushing a needle since 1990 — down the pressed-open allowance from the arm to the hip.

An inch and a half. Both sides. Folded in, pressed, overlocked at the raw edge and left there by somebody in a factory on a machine running at eight hundred stitches a minute, who had never met this woman and never would.

"Come and look at this," Alison said.

The woman came round the table, which people do not do.

"That's your seam allowance." She held it open with two fingers so the light came through the weave. "Inch and a half each side. That's three inch across the body of the dress, sat there in the cloth. It's been in there the whole time it's been in your boot."

"Is that not a mistake?"

"It's the opposite of a mistake." Her voice went plain, the way it goes when she is telling somebody a true thing about cloth, which is the only kind of thing she has ever been entirely sure of. "It costs them cloth to leave it and they leave it anyway. Because a maker leaves you room. Bodies alter. That's not a fault in the body, that's a fact about bodies, and a maker who knows her trade puts an inch and a half in the seam and says nowt about it." She let the cloth fall closed. "Nobody's body is a monument. It's not meant to stand still."

She took the dress to the machine and did not turn round for a moment.

Because it had gone through her, standing under eleven panes of glass with the green in her hands. Her own body had been altering itself these two years without a fitting. Nobody had chalked the line. Nobody had asked her to stand still. She had left room for every woman in this town and none whatever for herself.

It took forty minutes. The woman put it on behind Sonia's curtain and came out and fastened it, in the north light, and did not look at the mirror at all.

She looked at Alison.

And Alison, who has done this ten thousand times, turned to the machine and found something to do with her hands.
cliffhanger: Sonia Aktar's father's shears have not been out of their cloth since 2011.

title: The Yard Measure
segment_text:
## Chapter 16 — The Yard Measure

Sonia asked her at ten to nine, before the doors went up, which was itself a piece of information.

"Six kameez," she said. "My cousin's daughter. Eleven days."

"Who's doing them?"

"You are. I'll finish. My auntie was cutting and my auntie's hands have gone."

Alison heard herself say that she did alterations. She heard how it came out. It came out exactly like *I don't do curtains*, and she stood in her own draught with the sound of it and was ashamed in a way that had nothing to do with Sonia.

"I've not cut anything from flat since the bridal shop," she said. "That's twenty-six year."

"Twenty-six years of taking things apart," said Sonia. "You'll know how they go together."

Which was true and was not the point. To mend is to be handed a thing that already exists; whatever shape it is, the shape is not your fault. To cut is to decide. Alison had spent a lifetime being unable to be blamed and had not noticed until that minute that this was what it was.

"Right," she said. "Bring us the cloth."

Sonia went behind the counter and came back with a bolt of shot silk the colour of a wet slate roof, and then went again and came back with something else: a bundle of grey cloth, tied with tape, about eighteen inches long. She put it on the counter and unwrapped it without ceremony.

Shears. Black-handled, heavy, the blades long and blued at the shoulder.

"My father's," Sonia said. "He wrapped them in 2011. He sharpened them first. He knew he wasn't going to use them again, so he sharpened them, and then he put them away."

Alison did not pick them up straight off. She looked at them for a second on the counter and then she took them, and they sat in her hand with all their weight in the right place, the way a good tool does, so that they seemed to want to be closed.

They started at four, when the Saturday thinned. The hall went home around them by degrees — Kelly's shutter, Yusuf's wheel stopping, Margo's records going into their box with a noise like a deck of cards. Bernie came past at half five with two teas and no comment, which from Bernie is a bouquet. Hilary locked the north door and left the small one, and said, on her way out, that the lights over pitch 4 wanted an hour on the clock, and did not turn them off.

By seven there were two lamps on in the whole building and everything else was the black of glass at night. Six kameez, cut and stacked, the sleeves paired and pinned, the necks marked. Alison's knees had an opinion about the floor and her thumb had another and she had ignored both since half four.

Sonia measured a length off against the counter without looking down, thumb landing on the brass at thirty-six inches, where the metal has been worn to a shine by seventy years of thumbs — her father's, and his father's, and now, on the same inch, warm from the same shine, Alison's.
cliffhanger: Margo Denby needs something to wear on Wednesday, and will not say what for.

title: Margo's Green
segment_text:
## Chapter 17 — Margo's Green

"It's got to be Wednesday," Margo said, and put the frock on the table like a woman laying down a hand of cards.

It was green. Not the green of the columns, and not the green of Margo's thumbnail either; a hot, ringing, absolutely unrepentant green, cut in 1971 by somebody who had never heard of restraint, with a fitted bodice and a seam up the back you could have hung a door on.

"That is a frock," said Alison.

"That is a frock," Margo agreed. "I wore it eleven months. Every night for eleven months and twice on a Saturday, and it went in a case at the end of it and it's been in the case since, and now I want it on Wednesday."

"For what?"

"For Wednesday."

Alison let it go and picked the frock up instead, and turned it, and found what she had known she would find: the maker had been mean. Half an inch at the sides, if that. Whatever came out of this frock was going to have to come from somewhere else.

"There's not much in the seams," she said. "I can have the back seam over — move it entirely, take it out and set it again a full inch to the left, and let the sides go as far as they'll go. It'll want a new zip."

"Do it."

"You'll be a different shape in the back than you were."

"Love," said Margo, "I'm a different shape in the back than I was."

It took forty minutes and Margo talked for all of them. The band. Eleven months, 1971, a van with a hole in the floor you could watch the A62 through. Doncaster. A man from a record company who had, according to Margo, wept. She had sung, apparently, to nine hundred people in Sheffield, and then, when Alison put a pin in her mouth and raised an eyebrow, to something under two hundred, and then, after a while, said the true bit, quietly, with her hand flat on the cloth: that there had been four of them and they had been good, actually. Properly good. For about eleven months they had been the best thing in any room they walked into.

"Where are they now?"

"Dead, two of them. Barry's in Spain, which is worse." A beat. "It's Ray's on Wednesday. Rochdale. He played bass and he could not play bass, and I've decided I'm going in this, and they can all think what they like."

Alison put a pin in and said nothing and let the machine say it instead. The zip went in at twenty past. She pressed the new back seam over the ham and hung it on the hook by the north door, where the light gets it.

Margo stood and looked at it for a while with her arms folded. She put her hand out and took a fold of the skirt between finger and thumb — the chipped green nail against the green cloth, and the two greens not agreeing in any particular whatsoever, not one atom of them the same green.

"I'm aware," she said.
cliffhanger: There is a blazer in the bag with a name tape in it that is not anybody's name any more.

title: A Name Tape
segment_text:
## Chapter 18 — A Name Tape

Wednesday is half-day, so by one the hall had gone soft and echoing, the shutters coming down in ones and twos, Yusuf's wheel silent, Bernie counting the float out loud four stalls away because Bernie does everything out loud.

They came at ten past twelve: a mother in her forties and a fourteen-year-old in a coat with the sleeves over their hands. The blazer came out of a bag and went on the table.

"It's too big round the middle," the mother said. "It's been too big since we bought it. And there's — " she turned the collar over — "there's a tape in there."

Alison put her glasses on and got in under the lantern light. Woven tape, sewn into the neck facing with the small, tight, over-and-over hand of somebody who had been shown once and got it right. A name.

"Right," said Alison. "Two jobs, then. Waist and a tape."

"Yes," said the mother.

There is a question that belongs to Alison and a great many questions that do not, and thirty-six years at other people's shoulders had taught her the difference, which is not a thing you can be taught in a morning. She did not ask the ones that were not hers.

She looked at the fourteen-year-old, who was looking at the floor.

"What am I putting on the new one?" she said.

They told her.

"And how do you spell it?"

They spelled it. Alison wrote it on the docket in pencil, in capitals, and turned the docket round on the table so it faced them, the way she had turned ten thousand dockets round.

"Like that?"

"Yeah."

"Right."

She did the waist first, because it was the bigger job and the machine makes a noise, and a noise is somewhere to put a silence. Two inches out of the back seam, tapered, with the vent kept true — a blazer will forgive you a lot and will not forgive you a crooked vent — and the lining eased and dropped so it hung free, which is what a lining is for, so the outside can move without being told about it by the inside.

Then the tape. She unpicked the old one with the point of the quick-unpick, one stitch at a time, and it took longer than sewing it had, because that is the arithmetic of unpicking. It came away whole. She laid it on the table.

She sewed the new tape in with silk thread and did the ends first so it could not pull, and did over-and-over, small and tight, the same stitch that was already there, because there was no reason to do it differently and every reason not to.

"Six pound," she said. "Try it before you go."

They put it on. It fitted at the waist. They did up the button and put their hands in the pockets and stood there.

The mother picked the old tape up off the table, and folded it once, and put it in her purse, behind a card, and pressed the purse shut with both thumbs.

Alison saw her do it, and got on with clearing the table, and did not mention it. Not then. Not ever.
cliffhanger: The Singer has been making a noise since Tuesday, and this morning it stops.

title: The Motor
segment_text:
## Chapter 19 — The Motor

It had been making a noise since Tuesday — a small dry chirp at the top of the stroke, once every four or five inches of seam, that she had heard and had decided to hear later.

On Friday at twenty past nine it stopped. Not the noise. The machine.

She did the things you do. Plug, socket, the socket that Kelly's cart uses, the pedal, the pedal again, the belt, the belt tension, the plug once more because you always do the plug twice. The Singer sat on the deal in the north light, black and gold and older than she was and utterly finished with the whole business.

Alison stood behind her table and understood, in about the time it takes to boil a kettle, exactly what she was: a woman of fifty-two with a book of eleven jobs, seventy-two pounds a week going out, a redundancy she had promised herself she would not eat, and one machine. There was a new one in a shop in Halifax for four hundred pounds that was plastic and did a hundred stitches she would never use. She had a think about four hundred pounds. She did not like the think.

Yusuf came at half nine, because Bernie had told him, because Bernie tells everybody everything.

He did not ask. He put both arms round the machine, lifted it off the table with his knees and not his back, and carried it the length of the hall to pitch 19 with his chin over the balance wheel, and Alison walked behind it carrying the pedal and the flex.

He spread a sheet of newspaper. He took the plate off the end of the motor with a screwdriver he did not have to look for. Inside it was black — carbon dust, years of it, packed in the corners like soot in a flue. He blew it out. He turned the armature with one finger and listened, head over on one side, the way he listens to a key on the wheel.

"Brush," he said.

He held it up. A little block of carbon on a spring, worn down past its own shoulder to a stub the size of a back tooth, its spring gone slack behind it, no longer able to reach the thing it had been touching since 1949.

"It is one pound sixty," he said. "I have three."

"Yusuf."

"One pound sixty," he said, and would not be moved, and did not look up, and started cleaning the commutator with a scrap of emery on the end of a lolly stick.

He was forty minutes. He carried it back. She plugged it in and put a doubled scrap of calico under the foot and ran a seam, and it went, and it went sweet — the long low note it had had at Ellerby's under the north window, the note she had heard eight hours a day for twenty-six years and had stopped hearing about 2004.

Yusuf stood with his head on one side and listened for about four inches of it.

Then he nodded, before the seam had finished, and went back to pitch 19.
cliffhanger: On Saturday the traders are meeting in the hall after closing, and everybody has been asked.

title: A Show of Hands
segment_text:
## Chapter 20 — A Show of Hands

They put forty chairs out and twenty-two people came, which meant that for the whole of it there were eighteen empty chairs in the middle of the hall, and nobody sat on the front row, so it looked worse than it was.

Hilary had the urn on. Kelly had turned her chalkboard round and wiped the back of it, so that CAMOMILE was facing the wall, still spelled wrong, waiting.

Bernie went first and spoke for nine minutes. Nine. Alison timed it in the end because she had nothing else to do with her eyes. It was about her father-in-law, and the fish stall that used to be at pitch 11, and a man from the council in 1994 who had said a thing that had turned out not to be true, and somewhere in the middle of it there was one hard sentence — *they've been letting the roof go for eleven years and nobody's daft* — that nobody picked up, because it had nine minutes wrapped round it.

Margo proposed that they stop paying rent and put it in a jar until the roof was done. Hilary said that this was called withholding and had a legal meaning and would end the lease inside a month. Margo said she was aware. Somebody at the back said they should get the paper in. Somebody else said the paper was owned by the same lot.

Hilary read the lease out. Clause by clause, in the voice she reads everything in, which gives you nothing to lean on. Fourteen months. Break clause. Schedule of condition. The word *dilapidations*, which arrived in the hall like a stone through the glass and which four people asked about at once.

It was a mess. Alison sat at the end of the third row with her coat on and her hands in her sleeves and thought: this is what it looks like. Nobody stands up and says the thing. There is no thing. There are twenty-two people who are tired and it is quarter past eight and the urn has gone cold.

And then Sonia, who had not spoken, said, from the side, not standing up:

"They're not taking it off us. They're waiting for us to not want it."

The hall stopped.

Not dramatically. It was more that the noise in it changed key. Bernie, who had an answer to everything, did not have one. Yusuf turned round. Hilary put the lease down flat on her knee and looked at Sonia for a good three seconds and did not say a word, which from Hilary was the loudest thing that happened all night.

They stayed. That was the strange part. Somebody found the urn a plug that worked. At nine the lanterns went off because they are on a timer and nobody had the key for the timer, and the hall filled up instead with the orange of the streetlight on Corn Street coming down through eleven panes of dirty Victorian glass, and by that light, twenty-two people went on standing about in their coats, arguing, not leaving.

Alison was at the north door with her bag at ten past nine when she saw her.
cliffhanger: Pauline Craddock is at the north door at ten past nine, holding something she should not have.
